title: Tropical Storm Bertha Heads for Texas as Worst Flooding Hits States Hundreds of Miles Away
excerpt: Bertha's lopsided structure pushes its most damaging rainfall into the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee — far from the storm's Gulf Coast center — as it prepares for a final landfall on the upper Texas coast Thursday evening.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Tropical Storm Bertha is causing severe flooding far from its center, affecting the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee.
  • Warnings extend 600 miles along the Gulf Coast, from Louisiana to Texas, including Galveston.
  • Bertha's moisture plume is disrupting SpaceX's Starship launch planned for Thursday evening.
  • El Niño's wind shear has kept Bertha weak and lopsided, affecting the hurricane season's dynamics.

Tropical Storm Bertha is crawling toward a final landfall on the upper Texas coast Thursday evening, but the storm's most dangerous flooding is unfolding hundreds of miles from its center — across the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee.

As of the National Hurricane Center's 11 a.m. ET advisory Thursday, Bertha was centered about 35 miles southeast of Lake Charles, Louisiana, moving west at 10 mph with maximum sustained winds of 45 mph. The storm is expected to reach the upper Texas coast by late Thursday afternoon before dissipating inland over Texas by Friday.

A Storm Split in Two

Bertha has been lopsided from the start. Strong northeasterly wind shear — the hallmark of El Niño's influence on Atlantic hurricanes — has consistently blown the storm's heaviest thunderstorms well southwest of its center. That structure means the Gulf Coast near the center has seen relatively modest conditions: 2- to 3-foot storm surge from Pensacola, Florida, to southeast Louisiana, and wind gusts topping out around 50 mph.

The real damage is playing out to the northeast. A plume of tropical moisture linked to Bertha has funneled into a slow-moving cold front draped across the Southeast, producing flooding rain stretching from Tennessee to the mid-Atlantic.

"The heaviest rains with the entire storm are likely to impact south Texas."

— Weather Prediction Center, excessive rainfall discussion

In North Carolina, some areas have received a month's worth of rain in just a few days. Flash flood warnings hit Greensboro and Winston-Salem on Wednesday night after storms dumped up to 6 inches of rain in 12 hours. Flooding briefly closed a section of Interstate 40 northwest of Durham, according to the state's Department of Transportation. Near Knoxville, Tennessee, 5 inches fell in a few hours Wednesday morning, causing flash flooding.

Parts of the Chesapeake Bay region and Maryland recorded 6 to 8 inches of rain over 72 hours, according to the National Weather Service. The flood threat continues through Friday, with a Level 2 of 4 risk stretching from the Carolinas westward to northern Alabama.

Texas Braces for a Weakened but Wet Arrival

Along the immediate Gulf Coast, Bertha made its first landfall Wednesday afternoon near the Biloxi Wildlife Management Area in St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana, with winds peaking at 60 mph before weakening. Authorities in Mississippi, Louisiana, and Florida had opened sandbag distribution sites as red-flag warnings closed Gulf beaches to swimming.

Now heading for Texas, Bertha is forecast to bring 2 to 4 inches of rain, with isolated totals of 6 inches, to the Texas Gulf Coast and South Texas through Thursday night. Isolated flash flooding is possible, especially in urban areas, though dry ground conditions should limit the worst outcomes.

Houston, home to one of the largest Indian-American populations in the southern United States, is expected to escape significant impacts. "Could there be a 40 mph gust? Sure, but for the most part we're talking about conditions less than tropical storm force winds," Cameron Self, a National Weather Service meteorologist, told USA Today.

SpaceX Launch in Question

Bertha could also interfere with SpaceX's planned Starship rocket launch from its Starbase facility near the U.S.-Mexico border Thursday evening. The 90-minute launch window opens at 6:45 p.m. ET. SpaceX acknowledged on social media that "weather is currently a significant watch item for launch" as the storm pushes rain and wind toward the south Texas coast.

What Comes Next

Bertha is the second named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, following Tropical Storm Arthur in mid-June. NOAA forecasts a below-normal season overall, driven by El Niño's tendency to produce the wind shear that has kept Bertha weak.

"Wind shear is the number one calling card of El Niño," hurricane expert Michael Lowry of WPLG-TV told CNN. The pattern could suppress storm development across the Atlantic basin through the season's peak months in August and September.

For Gulf Coast communities still recovering from Arthur's flooding damage in Mississippi, Bertha's passage is a reminder that even weak tropical storms can produce outsized impacts — particularly when their moisture reaches far beyond the cone.
